title: Parables of the Kingdom and the Storm Stilled
summary: Teaching from a boat, Jesus tells the parable of the sower and explains privately that the mystery of the kingdom is given to his followers while outsiders hear only riddles. He adds sayings about a lamp and a measure and two more seed parables, the seed that grows by itself and the mustard seed. That evening, crossing the lake, a fierce storm threatens to swamp the boat, and Jesus, woken from sleep, rebukes the wind and the waves, leaving his terrified disciples asking who he is.
story: Chapter 3 ended with a divided response to Jesus: crowds flocked to him, his family doubted him, and the authorities said he was in league with Satan. Chapter 4 explains why. The parable of the sower describes a word that meets hard, shallow, crowded, and good soil, and the rest of Mark shows each of those responses in action. The chapter also marks a turn toward the disciples as the ones who receive private explanation. Then the story moves from teaching to action, and the storm scene raises the question that governs the next several chapters and the whole Gospel: “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?”
historical:
The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake about thirteen miles long and seven wide, lying roughly seven hundred feet below sea level in a basin surrounded by hills. Cool air sweeping down through the valleys can meet the warm air over the water and raise sudden, violent storms, a danger local fishermen knew well. In 1986, during a drought, the remains of a wooden fishing boat from around the first century were found in the mud near the lake's northwest shore. About twenty-seven feet long and seven wide, it could have carried a crew and passengers, and it gives a good picture of the kind of boat the disciples used, with a raised stern where a steersman sat and where Jesus could sleep on the helmsman's cushion.

The parables reflect Galilee's agricultural economy, which depended on grain and on small farms that often worked thin, stony soil on hillsides crossed by footpaths. Many families farmed land they did not own and paid rents and taxes in kind, so a good or bad harvest could decide whether a household survived the year.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East seed was often scattered by hand across a field, and some inevitably fell on the hard path, on patches where limestone lay just below a thin layer of soil, or among the roots of thorns. A yield of thirty, sixty, or a hundred times what was sown would have struck a Galilean farmer as extraordinary, well above an ordinary harvest, which is part of the parable's surprise. The mustard plant grown in the region could reach the height of a man or more in a season, large enough for birds to perch in, though it began from a tiny seed that was proverbial for smallness.

A parable (from the Greek word for placing things side by side) was a familiar teaching form in Israel, rooted in the Hebrew mashal, which covered proverbs, riddles, and illustrative stories. Parables draw on everyday life to say something about God, and they invite the hearer to work out the meaning and respond. Lamps were small clay oil lamps, and the basket was a grain measure, a bowl-shaped container that could cover a flame.
literary: Mark 4 is the first extended block of Jesus' teaching in Mark, and it is framed by the sea: Jesus teaches from a boat at the start and crosses the sea in a boat at the end. The parable of the sower (3 to 9) is followed by a private conversation and an explanation (10 to 20), which is sandwiched between the public telling and the other sayings. The repeated call to hear (verses 3, 9, 23, 24) signals the chapter's main theme: how one listens. The three seed parables all concern growth from small or hidden beginnings to a harvest. The storm story that follows turns the question from how the kingdom grows to who the king is, and the disciples, who were given the mystery of the kingdom, turn out to be as afraid and uncomprehending as outsiders.

outline.t: A lamp on a stand and the measure you use
The seed that grows by itself

doctrines.note: God's kingdom begins small and hidden, like seed in the ground or a mustard seed, and grows by God's power rather than human effort to a great harvest. The sower does not know how the seed grows; the growth is God's.

God reveals himself through his word, but hearing is not automatic. The same word falls on different soils, and those who receive it are given more. Understanding the kingdom is a gift given to those who come to Jesus.
Jesus asks his terrified disciples why they have no faith. Faith here is trust in Jesus' care and power even when he seems to be asleep, and the storm shows how quickly fear displaces it.

words.note: Parabole, parable, literally something placed alongside for comparison. In Mark it covers stories, short sayings, and riddles. Parables both reveal and conceal: they open the kingdom to those who ask and remain puzzles to those who stand outside.

Mysterion, mystery or secret. In the New Testament it does not mean a puzzle that cannot be solved but something once hidden in God's purposes and now revealed. The mystery of the kingdom is that God's reign has arrived in Jesus, in a hidden and unexpected form.

Sinapi, mustard, a plant grown in the region whose tiny seed produces a large shrub. The image contrasts the kingdom's small beginnings, a preacher and a handful of followers in Galilee, with its great end, where the birds nesting in its branches may echo Old Testament pictures of nations finding shelter (Ezekiel 17:23).

Hypakouo, to obey, from a word meaning to listen under. The same verb was used when the unclean spirits obeyed Jesus (1:27). Now the wind and sea obey him, and the disciples' question about who he is follows directly from that obedience.

christ: In the Old Testament, stilling the sea is something only God does. Psalm 107:23-30 describes sailors in a storm who cry to the Lord, and he makes the storm still and the waves hush. Psalm 89:9 says the Lord rules the raging sea. When Jesus rebukes the wind and it obeys, the disciples are right to be more afraid after the calm than during the storm: they are in the boat with someone who does what God does. The scene also echoes Jonah, asleep in a ship during a storm, though Jonah was fleeing God and Jesus is resting in him. In the parables Jesus is the sower of the word, and the kingdom whose hidden beginnings he describes is present in his own ministry.

hard.q: Does Jesus teach in parables so that people will not understand and be forgiven?
hard.a: Verses 11 and 12 are among the hardest in the Gospels. Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:9-10, where God commissions Isaiah to preach to a people who will not listen, and says that to outsiders everything comes in parables so that they may see without perceiving. Several points help. In Isaiah the words describe the effect of the prophet's preaching on a people who had already hardened themselves; God confirms a hardness they chose. The outsiders in Mark are defined by their response, since in chapter 3 the scribes and even Jesus' family stood outside while those around him were insiders, and anyone could come and ask, as the disciples do in verse 10. The parables are also said to be spoken to the extent that they could understand (verse 33), and a lamp is meant to be put on a stand (verse 21). Most interpreters read the passage as describing how parables work: they reveal to those who come seeking and they conceal from those who stand at a distance in judgment. Some read the purpose clause more strongly in terms of God's sovereign judgment. Either way the chapter's constant call is to hear, and its promise is that more will be given to those who do.

questions: Which kind of soil describes your response to God's word right now: hard, shallow, crowded, or open? What would help it become good soil?
The seed grows while the farmer sleeps, and he does not know how. How does that free you from anxiety about results in your work, your family, or your church?
The disciples asked Jesus, “Teacher, don’t You care that we are perishing?” When have you felt that way, and what does this story say to that fear?
